item.title: So you want to start something for animals: a map of the incubators
item.description:
Published on July 22, 2026 1:08 PM GMT

Tl;dr: A few years ago, if you wanted to found an animal advocacy organisation, there was basically one incubator. Now there are at least nine programs, plus several adjacent accelerators, and the hard part has shifted from finding support to choosing the right kind. This post maps the main options across focus, format, funding, and fit, so you can spend your energy on your idea rather than on decoding the landscape.

AI disclosure: I asked Claude to research the current programs and draft the comparison, then I verified the details, added a few more programs, added my own take on fit, and edited the result. Program details were checked against each organisation’s website in July 2026. If you spot any inaccuracies, please flag them in the comments, and I will correct them!

 

Recently I was chatting with a fellow board member, Cam, and we realised neither of us could confidently list all the incubation programs in animal advocacy anymore. That’s a good problem. When I started in this movement, “founding something” mostly meant one route or self-found. Now there’s a choice, and the programs serve various founding stages and needs. I’d love all aspiring founders to have the lay of the land and apply to the incubators that they are most suited to.

So here’s the map. At the end of the post, I’ve grouped programs by the question that matters most: what kind of founder are you, and what do you need?

A note on scope: I focus on programs whose goal is launching new organisations measured on impact for animals. Most build nonprofits, though a couple (Spring Innovation Fund, Myrias) also launch for-profit companies within a philanthropic model, where returns feed back into creating more ventures. Accelerators for commercial startups, like the ProVeg Incubator for alternative protein companies, get a brief note at the end.

Most of these programs run in cohorts, once a year or less, so at any given moment several will be closed. Sign up to each program's newsletter or follow them on LinkedIn, and you'll hear when the next round opens.

 

The programs

 

1. AIM (Charity Entrepreneurship)

The flagship. AIM’s Incubation Program is a free two-month, full-time program with a stipend that gives you a researched charity idea/problem space that’s very promising for a new org to enter. It matches you with a talented co-founder and provides up to ~$220,000 in seed funding. They’ve incubated 70+ organisations since 2018, including Shrimp Welfare Project and Fish Welfare Initiative, and others.

The big news: AIM is running its first incubation round focused exclusively on animal welfare in early 2027, in partnership with Aaron Boddy, co-founder of Shrimp Welfare Project.

Applications are open from August 3 until September 13, and you can sign up for an expression of interest to be notified. AIM has said publicly that it is bottlenecked by a lack of great animal founders, not ideas or funding. If you’ve ever assumed you’re not the founder type, or maybe you have founded something a while ago and are currently running it, that post is worth reading. It’s good to keep in mind that AIM is very competitive, but worth applying because top candidates may be referred for other high-impact roles in the movement.

Best for: People ready to go full-time on a rigorously researched idea, comfortable being matched to both an idea and a co-founder, and able to relocate or travel for the program. High intensity, high support, strongest funder network.

 

2. Kickstarting for Good

An 18-week program for nonprofits and impact initiatives transforming the food system, combining virtual phases (around 20 hours per week) with two in-person weeks in Berlin. It grew out of ProVeg and is now independent. The 2026 program runs from late July to late November. Graduates receive a minimum of $10,000 in seed funding, with up to $100,000 awarded by a jury of major funders at the Plant Food System Summit in Berlin in November, from a total pool of over $1 million this year, three times last year's. K4G has also secured matching grants, so graduates can double any funding they raise independently after the programme, and new for 2026, development grants of up to $12,000 go to promising applicants who don't make the cohort. You can apply with your own idea or take on one from their researched idea list. Alumni include Open Paws and the Farm Adaptation Network.

Best for: People with their own food-system or advocacy idea who can’t yet commit full-time. Note that there is no participation stipend: travel and accommodation for the Berlin weeks are covered, but your time is not.

Applications are closed for this year, but they usually open every year in spring. Join their mailing list to keep updated.

 

3. Welfare Matters (Farmed Animal Welfare Incubator)

A 12-week, full-time incubation programme launching locally-based nonprofits to improve farmed animal welfare in Southeast Asia, focused on Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam. The 2026 programme runs from early September to the end of November, mostly online with a two-week in-person component in the region, and this year's focus is layer hens and farmed fish, chosen through their own prioritisation research. The support package includes project-idea research, stipends to cover living costs, co-founder matching within the cohort, and a seed grant of up to $50,000 for accepted proposals, followed by a year of continued support. The 2024 cohort launched two organisations working on farmed duck welfare: Sentient Animals Vietnam and Across Species Project Indonesia. Note that FAWI runs roughly once every two years and the applications for this year are closed, so the next opportunity is likely 2028; their 14-week part-time fellowship (SEAFAWF) is the entry point in between.

Best for: Advocates based in or committed to Southeast Asia. The stipend and year of post-program support make this accessible.

Applications are closed for this year, but sign up to their newsletter to find out when their next cohort opens.

 

4. Animal Advocacy Africa

A training and incubation program for advocates launching farmed animal advocacy initiatives across Africa, where total farmed animal funding was around $2 million in 2022, less than 1% of the global total. Participants start with a training cohort (their second took 19 people from over 400 applicants), the strongest progress to an advanced phase to develop detailed project plans, and the best projects receive seed funding. Participants receive a stipend, and their Nigeria Fellowship covers accommodation for its in-person training week. Their first two cohorts incubated six new organisations, five still running, including Lumera in Zambia, which secured the country’s first conditional cage-free commitment. AAA also offers career support for advocates not ready to found, and regrants to African initiatives through its Catalyst Fund. Applications are closed for now, but sign up for their newsletter to be notified when they reopen.

Best for: Advocates based in Africa or willing to relocate there, especially those early in their journey who want training, network, and incubation in one package, with financial support along the way.

 

5. Myrias

A new venture studio rather than a classic incubator. Myrias builds nonprofits and for-profit companies targeting the largest and most neglected sources of animal suffering: farmed fish, insects, feeder rodents. Their prioritisation starts with China, where more than half the world’s farmed animals are raised. In a venture studio model, the studio generates and de-risks the ideas and recruits people to build them, so the entry point is often a role like Entrepreneur in Residence rather than a cohort application.

Best for: Experienced operators and builders who want to execute against a pre-researched, high-conviction thesis rather than develop their own idea, especially those with China or aquaculture context.

 

6. Rethink Priorities EOI (Special Projects and founder support)

Not an incubator, and RP says so themselves: their recent call for founders was an expression of interest, not a structured program with fixed slots. RP is looking for founders on frontier animal issues: wild animal welfare, invertebrates, aquatic animals, AI and animals, welfare technology, and neglected geographies with intensive farming but little advocacy infrastructure. Depending on fit, they offer 3 to 6 months of funded runway as a Special Project, an Entrepreneur in Residence role, or structured support to spin out as an independent organisation. Special Projects alumni include the Insect Institute, now a leading voice on insect farming, and the Center for Wild Animal Welfare, which secured a wild animal welfare debate and tabled amendments in the UK Parliament within months of launching.

RP’s key question to applicants is whether you’d switch to working on this full-time given the runway, and the funding is a pro-rated salary of $60,000 to $105,000 per year, designed to let you step away from your current role, although they may be open to part-time candidates. Their first expression-of-interest round closed in July 2026, but they’ve said there’s no fixed start date, and they want to hear from people who can’t start until next year, so it’s worth contacting them even between rounds.

Best for: Experienced people with a frontier-issue thesis (or strong motivation to develop one) who want institutional backing, research support, and a salary rather than a curriculum and cohort. RP notes that animal-specific background is not required.

 

7. Sentient Futures Project Incubator

A 10-week, fully remote, part-time program (5 to 10 hours per week) pairing fellows with mentors to build projects across animal welfare, artificial minds, and AI governance. The 2026 round runs from 31 August to 9 November, with applications closing 9 August. You can join a mentor’s pre-defined project or propose your own, and the goal is a finished standalone output rather than necessarily a new organisation. Alumni projects include an animal welfare benchmark merged into the UK AI Security Institute’s evaluation suite and Shared Roads, which engages governments on how driverless vehicle policy should account for animals.

Best for: People testing whether founding or independent work suits them, technical people bridging into advocacy, and anyone working at the intersection of AI and animals. The lowest-commitment entry point on this list, and it's unpaid, so it suits people who can carve out 5 to 10 hours a week alongside existing work or study.

 

8. Spring Innovation Fund

The newest entry, launched in 2026, is the first venture philanthropy studio dedicated to welfare tech: technology that improves animal welfare in ways that make commercial sense for producers to adopt. Spring is a 501(c)(3) that runs a paid three-month entrepreneur-in-residence program, after which selected founders may launch companies with roughly $500,000 in initial funding, plus follow-on support. Their pitch to founders is that salary, capital, co-founders, and initial research are all in place on day one. Focus areas include fish and crustacean welfare (their most active), hatchery and on-farm interventions, vaccines, and AI monitoring and breeding tools. Because donors take no equity and Spring recycles any returns into future ventures, it occupies unusual ground: you build a for-profit company, philanthropically backed, judged on welfare impact.

Best for: Builders, engineers, and commercially minded founders who want to create welfare technology companies rather than advocacy nonprofits, with the strongest day-one package on this list. You can do it with or without your own idea or even your established company.

 

9. The School for Moral Ambition (Food Fellowships)

Not an incubator, but a founding pathway hiding inside a placement fellowship. SMA, co-founded by Rutger Bregman in 2024, recruits mid-career professionals and embeds them in host organisations for six months; their first EU Food Fellows cohort graduated in April 2025, placed across 12 organisations spanning food, climate, and animal advocacy, with 83% still working in food system reform. The EU Food Transition Fellowship offers a monthly stipend of €4,000 gross plus a €1,000 monthly expense budget. And while the design is placement, founding keeps happening anyway: two fellows co-founded The Protein Project, which built a coalition of 90+ organisations influencing EU protein diversification policy. A US Food System Reform Fellowship launches in 2026, combining fundraising training with a six-month placement. There are no animal-only cohorts yet; the food fellowships sit within a broader protein transition frame, alongside SMA’s tobacco work.

Best for: Mid-career professionals from outside the movement who want a paid, structured transition into food system work, with founding as a possible outcome rather than the goal.

 

Which one is right for you?

The programs sort along four questions.

Do you have your own idea? If yes: Kickstarting for Good, or Sentient Futures. If no, and you want to be handed a rigorously researched one: AIM, AAA, Myrias, or Welfare Matters. Rethink Priorities and Spring Innovation Fund sit in both camps: they welcome founders with a specific idea and those motivated to develop one with their research team's support.

Can you go full-time? If yes: AIM, Myrias, Welfare Matters, Rethink Priorities, School for Moral Ambition. If no: Sentient Futures (lightest), AAA, or Kickstarting for Good. Rethink Priorities may be open to part-time candidates.

Where are you, and where do you want to work? Regional programs (AAA, Welfare Matters, Myrias) exist because context matters. If you’re based in those regions, they will likely serve you better than a global program, and the movement needs founders there most.

Can you afford to work unpaid? This question will help you decide which program is doable for your circumstances. Rethink Priorities, Spring Innovation Fund, School for Moral Ambition, and Myrias pay a salary or equivalent. Welfare Matters and AIM provide a cost-of-living stipend. AAA pays a modest stipend for part-time participation. Kickstarting for Good covers travel expenses. Sentient Futures does not currently provide a stipend.

 

If you’re unsure whether founding is for you at all

Start with the lowest-commitment option and produce something. A 10-week Sentient Futures project or a Kickstarting for Good application will teach you more about your fit than another six months of deliberation.

Speak to people who have founded something, or read/watch their accounts of what it’s like to found (here is mine!). You can also get some informal takes from previous incubator participants if you’d like to know what it’s really like to go through any particular incubator (e.g. you can ask on Hive in the help-requests channel).

 

What this list says about the movement

Five years ago the bottleneck was support infrastructure and funding. Today, by AIM’s own account, the bottleneck is founders. The infrastructure now exists across every commitment level, almost every region, and idea-ownership preference. If you’ve been waiting for the right on-ramp, it’s here, and there’s more than one.

 

A note on for-profit accelerators

If your idea is a company rather than a charity, you’re looking at a different ecosystem: the ProVeg Incubator (130+ alternative protein startups supported since 2018, currently running its free three-month Fast-track to Impact program) and Big Idea Ventures are the main entry points.

 

Hi, I’m Sofia Balderson. I lead Hive, a global community for people working to end factory farming. This post is from my Substack, Notes from the Margin, to share the messier, more personal reflections that don’t fit in formal updates. If you care about leading, belonging, or building something that matters (especially from the edges), you might enjoy sticking around.

Subscribe to get updated about my new posts.

Graduates receive a minimum of $10,000 in seed funding, with up to $100,000 awarded by a jury of major funders at the Plant Food System Summit in Berlin in November, from a total pool of over $1 million this year, three times last year's. K4G has also secured matching grants, so graduates can double any funding they raise independently after the programme, and new for 2026, development grants of up to $12,000 go to promising applicants who don't make the cohort. You can apply with your own idea or take on one from their researched idea list. Alumni include Open Paws and the Farm Adaptation Network.

Best for: People with their own food-system or advocacy idea who can’t yet commit full-time. Note that there is no participation stipend: travel and accommodation for the Berlin weeks are covered, but your time is not.

Applications are closed for this year, but they usually open every year in spring. Join their mailing list to keep updated.

 

3. Welfare Matters (Farmed Animal Welfare Incubator)

A 12-week, full-time incubation programme launching locally-based nonprofits to improve farmed animal welfare in Southeast Asia, focused on Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam. The 2026 programme runs from early September to the end of November, mostly online with a two-week in-person component in the region, and this year's focus is layer hens and farmed fish, chosen through their own prioritisation research. The support package includes project-idea research, stipends to cover living costs, co-founder matching within the cohort, and a seed grant of up to $50,000 for accepted proposals, followed by a year of continued support. The 2024 cohort launched two organisations working on farmed duck welfare: Sentient Animals Vietnam and Across Species Project Indonesia. Note that FAWI runs roughly once every two years and the applications for this year are closed, so the next opportunity is likely 2028; their 14-week part-time fellowship (SEAFAWF) is the entry point in between.

Best for: Advocates based in or committed to Southeast Asia. The stipend and year of post-program support make this accessible.

Applications are closed for this year, but sign up to their newsletter to find out when their next cohort opens.

 

4. Animal Advocacy Africa

A training and incubation program for advocates launching farmed animal advocacy initiatives across Africa, where total farmed animal funding was around $2 million in 2022, less than 1% of the global total. Participants start with a training cohort (their second took 19 people from over 400 applicants), the strongest progress to an advanced phase to develop detailed project plans, and the best projects receive seed funding. Participants receive a stipend, and their Nigeria Fellowship covers accommodation for its in-person training week. Their first two cohorts incubated six new organisations, five still running, including Lumera in Zambia, which secured the country’s first conditional cage-free commitment. AAA also offers career support for advocates not ready to found, and regrants to African initiatives through its Catalyst Fund. Applications are closed for now, but sign up for their newsletter to be notified when they reopen.

Best for: Advocates based in Africa or willing to relocate there, especially those early in their journey who want training, network, and incubation in one package, with financial support along the way.

 

5. Myrias

A new venture studio rather than a classic incubator. Myrias builds nonprofits and for-profit companies targeting the largest and most neglected sources of animal suffering: farmed fish, insects, feeder rodents. Their prioritisation starts with China, where more than half the world’s farmed animals are raised. In a venture studio model, the studio generates and de-risks the ideas and recruits people to build them, so the entry point is often a role like Entrepreneur in Residence rather than a cohort application.

Best for: Experienced operators and builders who want to execute against a pre-researched, high-conviction thesis rather than develop their own idea, especially those with China or aquaculture context.

 

6. Rethink Priorities EOI (Special Projects and founder support)

Not an incubator, and RP says so themselves: their recent call for founders was an expression of interest, not a structured program with fixed slots. RP is looking for founders on frontier animal issues: wild animal welfare, invertebrates, aquatic animals, AI and animals, welfare technology, and neglected geographies with intensive farming but little advocacy infrastructure. Depending on fit, they offer 3 to 6 months of funded runway as a Special Project, an Entrepreneur in Residence role, or structured support to spin out as an independent organisation. Special Projects alumni include the Insect Institute, now a leading voice on insect farming, and the Center for Wild Animal Welfare, which secured a wild animal welfare debate and tabled amendments in the UK Parliament within months of launching.

RP’s key question to applicants is whether you’d switch to working on this full-time given the runway, and the funding is a pro-rated salary of $60,000 to $105,000 per year, designed to let you step away from your current role, although they may be open to part-time candidates. Their first expression-of-interest round closed in July 2026, but they’ve said there’s no fixed start date, and they want to hear from people who can’t start until next year, so it’s worth contacting them even between rounds.

Best for: Experienced people with a frontier-issue thesis (or strong motivation to develop one) who want institutional backing, research support, and a salary rather than a curriculum and cohort. RP notes that animal-specific background is not required.

 

7. Sentient Futures Project Incubator

A 10-week, fully remote, part-time program (5 to 10 hours per week) pairing fellows with mentors to build projects across animal welfare, artificial minds, and AI governance. The 2026 round runs from 31 August to 9 November, with applications closing 9 August. You can join a mentor’s pre-defined project or propose your own, and the goal is a finished standalone output rather than necessarily a new organisation. 8. Spring Innovation Fund

The newest entry, launched in 2026, is the first venture philanthropy studio dedicated to welfare tech: technology that improves animal welfare in ways that make commercial sense for producers to adopt. Best for: Builders, engineers, and commercially minded founders who want to create welfare technology companies rather than advocacy nonprofits, with the strongest day-one package on this list. You can do it with or without your own idea or even your established company.

 

9. The School for Moral Ambition (Food Fellowships)

Not an incubator, but a founding pathway hiding inside a placement fellowship. Best for: Mid-career professionals from outside the movement who want a paid, structured transition into food system work, with founding as a possible outcome rather than the goal.

 

Which one is right for you?

The programs sort along four questions.

Do you have your own idea? If yes: Kickstarting for Good, or Sentient Futures. If no, and you want to be handed a rigorously researched one: AIM, AAA, Myrias, or Welfare Matters. Rethink Priorities and Spring Innovation Fund sit in both camps: they welcome founders with a specific idea and those motivated to develop one with their research team's support.

Can you go full-time? If yes: AIM, Myrias, Welfare Matters, Rethink Priorities, School for Moral Ambition. If no: Sentient Futures (lightest), AAA, or Kickstarting for Good. Rethink Priorities may be open to part-time candidates.

Where are you, and where do you want to work? Regional programs (AAA, Welfare Matters, Myrias) exist because context matters. If you’re based in those regions, they will likely serve you better than a global program, and the movement needs founders there most.

Can you afford to work unpaid? This question will help you decide which program is doable for your circumstances. Rethink Priorities, Spring Innovation Fund, School for Moral Ambition, and Myrias pay a salary or equivalent. Welfare Matters and AIM provide a cost-of-living stipend. AAA pays a modest stipend for part-time participation. Kickstarting for Good covers travel expenses. Sentient Futures does not currently provide a stipend.

 

If you’re unsure whether founding is for you at all

Start with the lowest-commitment option and produce something. A 10-week Sentient Futures project or a Kickstarting for Good application will teach you more about your fit than another six months of deliberation.

Speak to people who have founded something, or read/watch their accounts of what it’s like to found (here is mine!). You can also get some informal takes from previous incubator participants if you’d like to know what it’s really like to go through any particular incubator (e.g. you can ask on Hive in the help-requests channel).

 

What this list says about the movement

Five years ago the bottleneck was support infrastructure and funding. Today, by AIM’s own account, the bottleneck is founders. The infrastructure now exists across every commitment level, almost every region, and idea-ownership preference. If you’ve been waiting for the right on-ramp, it’s here, and there’s more than one.

 

A note on for-profit accelerators

If your idea is a company rather than a charity, you’re looking at a different ecosystem: the ProVeg Incubator (130+ alternative protein startups supported since 2018, currently running its free three-month Fast-track to Impact program) and Big Idea Ventures are the main entry points.

item.title: Introducing Impact List: a ranking of philanthropists by expected lives saved
item.description:
Published on July 22, 2026 2:04 PM GMT

TL;DR: I'm releasing a website that ranks philanthropists according to EA principles and research, and allows users to re-rank the list using their own assumptions. I'd like feedback and help making it better. I'd especially like ideas for how to make the results more trustworthy. Funding may be available.

I recently built Impact List (impactlist.xyz), a site which ranks people by their positive impact via donations. 

The goal is to make the list popular enough that people care about their ranking on it, so that it influences their decisions about where and how much to donate. A secondary goal is influencing people (whether or not they appear on the list) by making them more aware of the large differences in the cost to save a life depending on where money is donated.

The site uses QALYs as the common currency of value, but this doesn't mean it's limited to considering only effects on health/lifespan. The goal is to consider effects of any type and convert them to human-QALY-equivalents.

I wrote more about the motivation and theory of this project four years ago in this post. 

What Impact List is

The core of the site is a ranking of (currently 73) wealthy philanthropists by their expected impact via donations. 

Each donor has their own page showing all their donations (along with the impact of each donation), and aggregate stats by cause area. Users can toggle between 'donations' and 'lives saved' to visualize differences in effectiveness between cause areas. The internal QALY metric is converted into lives saved by defining one life = 80 QALYs.

I've split all donations into 28 cause areas, each with their own 'cost to save a life' value. 

There's also a page for every recipient (charitable organization), which can have its own 'cost per life' value if it's more or less effective than the cause area average. Each cause area and customized recipient has a page with a detailed justification for how the math was done to arrive at the cost per life, and where assumptions are explicitly listed. 

The estimates are of course very approximate, and will be controversial. I make heavy use of LLMs to do this research, encouraging them to synthesize existing (often EA) analysis. Users who disagree with any of the default parameter values can edit them.

Users can also edit global parameters specifying their time horizon, assumptions about population growth, and the discount rate. 

After entering their own assumptions, users can create shareable links. This allows others to see what Impact List would look like given person X's worldview. 

I'd eventually like to add worldviews from notable researchers or organizations, but I'm starting with just a handful of worldviews based on simple tweaks to the defaults:

There's also a calculator feature where people can enter their past donations and/or donations they're considering and see where they'd rank on the list, given those donations.

What I'd like help with

If you see something below that you want to help with, comment on this post, DM me, or join the Discord. 

Improving the process of effectiveness estimation

Few people are going to dive into the details of the effectiveness estimates and verify for themselves that the research is high quality. So it's not enough that the estimates be excellent. People need to be able to easily understand and trust the process that leads to the estimates.

The current process is LLM-driven, opaque (users can't see the prompts that lead to the estimates and they can't see how feedback is processed), and dependent on the judgments of someone (me) without any reputation as a researcher.  I've tried to partly compensate for this by making the justifications explicit about which assumptions are being made, and tried to make the reasoning as clear as possible, but I expect it'll be very hard to generate enough trust using the existing process.

A few things that could help:

  1. Incorporating something like X's Community Notes on each individual assumption[1], or otherwise making user feedback more of a first-class thing.
  2. Getting people/orgs who have already built up trust to publish their worldviews, and doing some blending between them.
  3. Making the estimation process more auditable, including giving details on currently-behind-the-scenes LLM interactions.
  4. Coming up with some council-of-LLMs framework that minimizes special privilege given to any person or group's judgment. Even if LLMs aren't good enough for people to trust something like this now, maybe they will be in N months.

If you have ideas in this area, please share in the comments. I see this as the most important obstacle to the site becoming popular.

Improving the individual effectiveness estimates

The effectiveness estimates for all cause areas are mostly based on research from LLMs (frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI). I've also done some manual review and back and forth with the LLMs to refine the estimates. The LLMs rely a lot on existing EA research, but the quality of the analysis is pretty uneven and could probably be improved a lot by putting expert human researchers in the loop.

I'd like these estimates to become the best place to look for a synthesis of all effectiveness research that EAs have done (or found).

If you have expertise in cause area effectiveness research, and especially if you're an expert in some particular cause area, it would be great if you'd be willing to help improve the estimates.

Making the site more usable and beautiful

I think the site looks OK now, but not great (especially on mobile). If you have UI skills/taste and want to make the site look better, let me know.

Getting notable people and organizations to publish their own worldviews 

As mentioned above, the site allows anyone to make their own customized set of assumptions and create a shareable link to the rankings using these assumptions. 

For notable people/orgs, I'd like to add these links as curated options for all users, so people could see Impact List according to Carl Shulman, Rethink Priorities, etc.

If you're a notable researcher or work in a well-respected EA org, and you also want this to happen, please get in touch.

Go-to-market advice

How should we actually make the site popular? In my post introducing this project I talked about some ideas for how to do this, but I'm pretty uncertain about the right path here. 

My sense is that the quality of the site should be significantly higher before I try to popularize this beyond EA/rationalist audiences, but it'd be nice to have a distribution plan soon to guide the other site-improvement decisions.

Suggestions for high-impact people currently not on the list

Everyone currently on the list is well known, but that's not a requirement. Feel free to nominate yourself (if your donations can be proven to the satisfaction of a skeptical reader) or someone else I missed.

Improvements to the underlying data model and estimation framework

See Appendix A below for details on how this works. I've tried to strike a balance between simplicity and expressive power, but I'm not sure I've picked the right tradeoff or whether I'm on the Pareto frontier.

Funding may be available

A couple of funders have offered to give me grants for this work. I haven't accepted any yet, but if you want to work on Impact List and you want to be paid, these grantors may be willing to make that happen.  

Getting involved

The project has a Discord. You can also submit pull requests via GitHub. Feel free to DM me on this forum.

You can keep up with the project on Twitter.

Above I've listed what I think I most need, but I may be wrong. I'm happy for all sorts of help or feedback.

Thanks to Austin Chen, Ryan Kidd, Kim Korte, Nathan Young, plex, and Laszlo Treszkai for discussion and feedback about the site. 

Appendix A: How effectiveness is modeled

The details are on GitHub. This is a simplified overview. 

Each cause area or charitable organization has one or more 'effects', which define how money translates into QALYs. There are two types of effects, standard effects and population effects, and each effect has several parameters. 

Standard Effects

The most intuitive type. The more money you spend, the more impact you get. The parameters are:

  • Cost per QALY: How much money it costs to produce one QALY
  • Start time: Years after donation before the effect begins
  • Duration: How many years the effect lasts (benefits are assumed to be evenly distributed)

Population Effects

Effects where money donated changes the probability of some event. This is used to model x-risks, pandemics, etc. The parameters are:

  • Cost per microprobability: How much it costs to change the likelihood of an event by 1 in 1,000,000.
  • Population fraction affected: What fraction of the population is impacted if the event occurs
  • Welfare change per person per year: estimated welfare change per affected person per year, in QALYs. Positive values mean the funded work makes a bad event less likely or a good event more likely; negative values mean it does the opposite.
  • Start time / Duration: Same meaning as for the standard effects

Overrides and multipliers

A recipient organization which is part of some cause area can override the parameters of that cause area, to indicate that the recipient is especially effective or ineffective. 

Recipient organizations can also have their parameters defined as a multiple of a parameter of the cause area it belongs to. The site's UI currently hides the ability to express parameters in terms of multiples for simplicity, though I'd like to re-add this to the UI at some point.

Time

The model is capable of handling time-based effects, which allows specifying different levels of effectiveness for a cause/recipient depending on when the donation was made. For instance a donation to MIRI today may have a very different impact than a donation to MIRI in 2012. The current version of the site doesn't make use of time-based effects, but they're available and documented on GitHub.

Motivation for these choices

This model gives each effect a 'shape' over time that we can integrate over to get the total value. This allows assumptions about the future population, discount rate, and time horizon to be separated out from cause-specific assumptions.

I could have made these shapes more complex by having options for exponential or linear decay of effects, but I think it's not worth the extra complexity. Every effect-shape in this model is a simple rectangle.

Appendix B: Current limitations and uncertainties

  • I currently only consider impact via donations. I'd eventually like to include all of a person's positive and negative externalities, including via businesses they've created, via politics, etc.
  • The site's estimates are very uncertain, and this could probably be quantified and communicated better to non-EAs, possibly along with some explanation of why uncertain estimates are still valuable.
  • As seen in Appendix A, the underlying model is fairly simple.
  • Although the site infrastructure supports it, I don't currently distinguish average effectiveness from marginal effectiveness or account for effectiveness changes over time.
  • I don't try to measure fungibility or crowding-out/in effects.
  • I use LLMs to gather donation data for each person using this skill, and it seems to work fairly well, but not perfectly.
  • Not all donations are public, so the data is missing some donations. However because it's usually in the interest of both the donor and the recipient to publicize donations (the donor gets status and to raise the profile of a cause they care about, the recipient gets attention from other potential donors), my guess is that this effect isn't huge.
  • I don't count pledges, but I fully count donations that a person makes to a charitable foundation or fund that they control. In some cases this seems like what we want, but in others it probably overstates the donor's impact. This could be addressed by giving these foundations customized lower effectiveness estimates, but I haven't done that yet.
  • The cause area breakdown for multi-cause recipients like The Gates Foundation is based on estimates from LLMs, not on classifying all of the grants that they've made.
  • I'm unsure whether the 28 cause areas that I've picked are the best way to carve up the space.
  • Inflation isn't yet adjusted for.

 

 

  1. ^

    Thanks to Nathan Young for the suggestion and for discussions around this idea.

  • Although the site infrastructure supports it, I don't currently distinguish average effectiveness from marginal effectiveness or account for effectiveness changes over time.
  • I don't try to measure fungibility or crowding-out/in effects.
  • I use LLMs to gather donation data for each person using this skill, and it seems to work fairly well, but not perfectly.
  • Not all donations are public, so the data is missing some donations. However because it's usually in the interest of both the donor and the recipient to publicize donations (the donor gets status and to raise the profile of a cause they care about, the recipient gets attention from other potential donors), my guess is that this effect isn't huge.
  • I don't count pledges, but I fully count donations that a person makes to a charitable foundation or fund that they control. In some cases this seems like what we want, but in others it probably overstates the donor's impact. This could be addressed by giving these foundations customized lower effectiveness estimates, but I haven't done that yet.
  • The cause area breakdown for multi-cause recipients like The Gates Foundation is based on estimates from LLMs, not on classifying all of the grants that they've made.
  • I'm unsure whether the 28 cause areas that I've picked are the best way to carve up the space.
  • Inflation isn't yet adjusted for.
